case_studies.title: All Smoke, No Alarm: Oracle Signals in Agent-Authored Test Code
case_studies.abstract: Software practitioners increasingly use AI coding agents that generate test code alongside production code in open source pull requests (PRs). Recent studies report more than 932,000 agent-authored PRs across more than 116,000 repositories, yet whether their test files contain meaningful verification logic remains underexplored. Test files lacking explicit assertions execute code without verifying behavior, so quality gates based on test-file presence overestimate verification strength. The goal of this paper is to help practitioners assess the verification strength of agent-authored patches b
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of assessing the quality of test code generated by AI coding agents in open source projects. The authors built a method to evaluate the verification strength of agent-authored test code. The result helps practitioners identify if the test files contain meaningful verification logic or not.

case_studies.title: Knowledge Reutilization in Meta-Reinforcement Learning
case_studies.abstract: Meta-reinforcement learning enables fast adaptation by extracting shared structure from related tasks, but existing end-to-end methods often couple task inference with embodiment-specific control. This coupling can obscure non-parametric task semantics, reduce sample efficiency, and limit cross-agent reuse. We propose a meta-knowledge reutilization framework that learns task-level knowledge on a dynamics-simplified agent and transfers it to heterogeneous agents. The framework uses a Bayesian non-parametric prior to organize latent task modes and a high-level policy to generate task-level magni
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of limited cross-agent reuse in meta-reinforcement learning by building a meta-knowledge reutilization framework. The framework allows for task-level knowledge to be learned on one agent and transferred to other agents. The result is improved sample efficiency and faster adaptation to new tasks.

case_studies.abstract: We evaluate the adversarial robustness of two frontier large language models (LLMs) developed by Anthropic, Fable 5 and Opus 4.8, against four families of automated jailbreak attack across 7 826 harmful intents spanning a ten-category harm taxonomy. Using the HackAgent red-teaming framework, hundreds of thousands of adversarial attempts were generated and every apparent success was independently re-adjudicated by a panel of three judge models (majority vote). case_studies.summary: This research evaluates the security of two large language models against automated attacks, finding that while they resist most attacks, there are still vulnerabilities. case_studies.title: Seeing Is Not Screening: Multimodal Hidden Instruction Attacks on Agent Skill Scanners
case_studies.abstract: Agent skills are emerging as an important attack surface in LLM-based systems. Through an empirical study of existing skill scanners, we find that current defenses primarily rely on textual descriptions, manifests, and source code as the main signals for security analysis, which can leave visually conveyed malicious intent insufficiently examined. This creates a practical blind spot: harmful operational instructions hidden in images may bypass scanning while still being recoverable by multimodal agents during deployment. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of hidden malicious intent in images that can bypass current security scanners, the authors built a tool called SkillCamo to investigate this threat, and the result shows that harmful operational instructions can be hidden in images and recovered by multimodal agents. The study focuses on agent skills in LLM-based systems, which may not be directly relevant to general cloud infrastructure management. However, it may impact organizations using LLM-based systems with multimodal agents.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM-based systems with multimodal agents, here is what to do: review your current security scanners to ensure they inspect visual content, assess the risk of hidden malicious instructions in images, and consider implementing additional security measures to address this blind spot.

case_studies.title: Evaluating Open-Source LLMs for Multi-Label ATT&CK Technique Classification on CTI Reports
case_studies.abstract: Classifying Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) using MITRE Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge (ATT&CK) is essential for proactive defense, but historically required extensive human effort. Pre-Large Language Model (LLM) automation sped up this process, but could not resolve the complex language and multi-step attack patterns found in unstructured CTI reports. LLMs addressed previous limitations by using contextual reasoning to understand unstructured text. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of classifying Cyber Threat Intelligence reports by building an open-source Large Language Model that can handle complex language and multi-step attack patterns, resulting in more accurate and efficient classification. The model uses contextual reasoning to understand unstructured text, improving upon previous automation methods. This research aims to enhance proactive defense against cyber threats.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cyber threat intelligence systems, here is what to do: review your current classification methods, consider integrating open-source LLMs into your workflow, and evaluate the potential benefits of improved contextual reasoning for multi-label ATT&CK technique classification.
